strengths: Addresses a fundamental and challenging problem in embodied vision and robotics: amodal 3D object reconstruction under severe occlusion during in-hand manipulation.

Technically sound integration of physical interaction signals (proprioception and multi-contact touch) mapped into a shared camera-aligned 3D coordinate frame, providing explicit geometric constraints (non-interpenetration and contact consistency).
Effective formulation of physical constraints both as auxiliary losses during conditional flow-matching fine-tuning and as test-time decoder guidance during ODE sampling.

Solid empirical evaluation stratified across occlusion severity levels against competitive baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D), complemented by real-world validation on a physical humanoid platform with an unseen end-effector and tactile sensor setup.
weaknesses: The 3D grid resolution of $64^3$ is relatively coarse, particularly when the shared grid must encompass both the robotic hand and the manipulated object, which limits fine geometric details and thin structures.

In the real-world evaluation (Table 3), the performance improvements over the vision-only baseline (SAM3D) are modest; SAM3D achieves a higher F@0.02 (0.225 vs. 0.186) and slightly better EMD (0.185 vs. 0.190), reflecting the method's sensitivity to hand-eye calibration and kinematic errors in real setups.
Stage B (appearance and surface refinement) is largely descriptive and lacks rigorous quantitative evaluation regarding texture fidelity or photometric consistency compared to the baseline pipelines.

strengths: Well-motivated integration of physical cues (proprioception and multi-contact touch) into a 3D generative model to tackle the fundamentally ill-posed problem of amodal object reconstruction under heavy hand occlusion.

Formulating both the posed end-effector and the object within a shared, camera-aligned signed distance field (SDF) grid provides an elegant and mathematically sound framework for enforcing differentiable non-interpenetration and contact consistency losses during training and inference guidance.

Comprehensive evaluation across varying degrees of occlusion (stratified bins B1–B5), demonstrating clear advantages over vision-only baselines (Amodal3R and SAM3D) particularly in severe occlusion regimes.

Inclusion of hardware validation on a physical humanoid platform featuring an unseen end-effector morphology, demonstrating cross-embodiment feasibility and practical relevance for robotic manipulation.
weaknesses: Coarse grid resolution: Sharing a single 64^3 voxel grid between the robot end-effector and the object significantly limits the effective resolution dedicated to the object, restricting the capture of thin structures and fine details.

Sensitivity to calibration and kinematic drift: As acknowledged in the text and visible in Fig. 4 / Fig. A2, the method depends heavily on accurate hand forward kinematics and hand-camera extrinsics; slight calibration errors can propagate and cause hand-object misalignments.

Computational overhead of physical guidance at inference time: Differentiable decoder guidance requires repeatedly decoding latents to 3D SDFs and backpropagating gradients during Euler integration steps, but the paper does not report inference latency, memory consumption, or the computational cost of this guidance loop.
Limited real-world quantitative scale: The real-robot evaluation is conducted on only 5 selected YCB objects, which restricts the empirical breadth of the sim-to-real and cross-embodiment claims.

Performance trade-off under low occlusion: In the least-occluded regime (bin B1), the vision-only baseline (SAM3D) outperforms the proposed method on precision metrics like F@0.02 (0.265 vs. 0.215), suggesting that the discretized SDF prior may oversmooth fine surface geometry when visual evidence is readily available.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: Leveraging physical interaction signals (proprioception and multi-contact tactile sensing) to constrain amodal 3D generative reconstruction addresses an intrinsic ambiguity of vision-only methods during dexterous in-hand manipulation.

Technically sound formulation: Integrating camera-aligned metric SDFs with a Structure-VAE enables differentiable formulation of physical interaction losses (contact consistency and non-interpenetration) for both flow-matching finetuning and test-time Euler sampling guidance.

Thorough evaluation across occlusion levels: The experimental protocol stratifies performance by occlusion severity, clearly showing that while vision-only baselines degrade severely under heavy occlusions, the proposed multimodal physics-grounded approach maintains robust geometry and pose estimation.

Real-robot deployment and embodiment transfer: The authors validate the method on a physical humanoid platform equipped with an unseen end-effector and tactile sensors, demonstrating practical applicability and cross-embodiment generalization.
weaknesses: Resolution bottlenecks from shared grid representation: Discretizing the shared hand-object domain into a fixed 64^3 grid restricts the effective resolution allocated to the object. This likely explains why the fine-grained F-score (F@0.02) trails SAM3D across several regimes, limiting high-frequency geometric detail recovery.

Missing isolated ablation on test-time physical guidance: While the paper presents sensing ablations (Vision-only vs. No-Touch vs. Full) and qualitative guidance progression (Fig. A3), it lacks quantitative results isolating the relative impact of test-time physical guidance versus training-time auxiliary losses alone.

Limited scale of real-world quantitative evaluation: The real-robot experiment is evaluated on only 5 objects, where sensor noise and hand-eye calibration discrepancies visibly affect performance, showing minor degradation compared to SAM3D on metrics such as F@0.02 and EMD.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated multimodal formulation that leverages tactile sensing and robot proprioception as geometric constraints to resolve fundamental visual ambiguities under severe hand occlusion.

Sound technical design: representing the scene via a camera-aligned, pose-aware SDF grid allows seamless integration of non-interpenetration and contact-consistency terms both as training loss functions and test-time guidance via the Structure-VAE decoder.

Comprehensive experimental validation in simulation across stratified occlusion bins, demonstrating consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over strong baselines (Amodal3R and SAM3D), especially in pose accuracy and high-occlusion regimes.
Real-world demonstration on a physical humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector and tactile sensors, exhibiting generalization across different robot embodiments.

Thorough ablation study evaluating the relative importance of individual sensing modalities (touch vs. proprioception), the utility of physics losses and guidance, and the robustness against sensor/kinematic calibration noise.
weaknesses: The 64^3 volumetric grid resolution is relatively coarse, particularly because the shared canonical domain must enclose both the robotic hand and the object, limiting the fine geometric details that can be captured in Stage A.

In the real-world evaluation (Table 3), the performance margin over SAM3D is modest (e.g., F@0.02 is lower than SAM3D), largely due to sensitivity to camera-to-hand calibration and forward kinematics error.
Minor presentation polish issues in the appendix (e.g., typographical error on page 27: 'it’s tryue that different seed can yield better results').

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem at the intersection of computer vision and robotics: amodal, metric-scale 3D object reconstruction and pose estimation under heavy occlusion during robotic manipulation.

Technically sound formulation combining a pose-aware camera-aligned SDF representation in a Structure-VAE latent space with flow-matching diffusion, naturally unifying visual, proprioceptive, and tactile modalities in a shared 3D frame.
Effective integration of physical constraints both during training (non-interpenetration and contact consistency losses) and at test-time via differentiable decoder guidance.

Comprehensive empirical validation across simulation (stratified across 5 occlusion bins) and real-world experiments on a humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector morphology, demonstrating cross-embodiment generalization.
Solid ablations isolating the contributions of tactile distance fields vs. binary contacts, guidance, and robustness to kinematic, mask, and sensor noise.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to kinematic and calibration errors: As highlighted in the ablation study and real-robot qualitative results (e.g., Fig. 4, third row), errors in camera-to-hand calibration and forward kinematics directly propagate to the reconstruction, leading to hand-object misalignment.

Resolution limitations: Discretizing the shared hand-object bounding volume onto a fixed 64^3 grid restricts the effective resolution available for the object, potentially losing thin geometric structures and concavities before Stage B refinement.

Experimental details for real-world ground truth: Section 4.3 and Appendix B.1 present quantitative metrics on 5 real YCB objects, but the exact protocol for obtaining real ground-truth 3D meshes and their ground-truth 6D poses during grasping is not sufficiently detailed.

Reliance on 2D instance masks: The framework assumes reliable visible-object and occluder masks (Mo, Mh) as inputs, which can be noisy or difficult to obtain under severe contact and cluttered interaction scenarios.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: addressing metric-scale amodal 3D object reconstruction and pose estimation under severe in-hand occlusion by fusing vision with physical interaction cues (proprioceptive hand pose and multi-contact tactile sensing).

Principled technical design: representing the scene as a camera-aligned SDF enables differentiable physics-grounded constraints (non-interpenetration and contact consistency) that are used effectively both during flow-matching finetuning and as test-time guidance.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: the approach is evaluated on simulated manipulation across multiple occlusion tiers, tested for cross-embodiment generalization on a real humanoid robot, and validated on human grasp benchmarks (DexYCB) against specialized methods.

Detailed ablation and robustness analysis: the paper thoroughly isolates each sensing modality, investigates the impact of distance fields vs. binary contact, studies test-time guidance, and quantifies sensitivity to kinematic, tactile, and segmentation mask noise.
weaknesses: Resolution bottlenecks: Discretizing the shared hand-object domain into a fixed 64^3 grid restricts the effective spatial resolution dedicated to the object, limiting the recovery of intricate geometry or thin structures prior to downstream refinement.

Sensitivity to kinematic calibration: As highlighted by the ablation in Table 4 and qualitative examples in the supplementary material (Fig. A2, Fig. A4), the framework is noticeably sensitive to camera-to-hand extrinsics and forward kinematics noise, which causes alignment errors and occasional generative failures.

Mixed real-world performance against baselines: In the real-robot quantitative evaluation (Table 3), although the proposed method achieves the best Voxel IoU and normal consistency, SAM3D achieves a superior F@0.02 score (0.225 vs. 0.186) and slightly better EMD, indicating that real-world sensor noise narrows the practical advantage over strong vision-only models.

Limited scale of real-world validation: The physical hardware evaluation is restricted to only five YCB objects, which limits the breadth of conclusions regarding general real-world deployment across diverse object topologies and surface textures.
